verdicts.question: For investors, should Luma.Green quote e-waste at 1.4 Mt (CPCB, FY2024-25) or 6.19 Mt (NITI Aayog, 2024)? Explain how each is measured and which to lead with. What figure is defensible for India's recycling market size and for the number of waste pickers?
verdicts.problems: VERIFICATION STATUS: none of the 14 cited sources could be confirmed by snippet in this pass (WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200, page fetches refused, repo grep blocked by the permission classifier). Everything below is a knowledge-based audit, not a snippet check. (1) Competing official series not surfaced: a MoEFCC Rajya Sabha reply of December 2024 (PIB) gave e-waste generation as 10.14 lakh t in 2019-20 rising to 17.51 lakh t in 2023-24 (the widely reported '72.54% rise'); the answer's 12,54,286.55 t for FY2023-24 (cited to the 11 Aug 2025 reply) is a different, lower CPCB series for the same year. The answer flags a processing-figure conflict but not this generation-figure conflict, and an investor who Googles 'India e-waste 2023-24' will find 17.51 lakh t first. The likely explanation (old series = annual-report/all-EEE basis, new series = EPR-portal sales-times-life basis under the 2022 Rules) is plausible but was not confirmed by snippet. (2) The March 2026 FY2025-26 pair (14.14 lakh t generated, 9.79 lakh t recycled) is cited only to a PTI wire on NewsDrum; not confirmed by snippet, and no PIB/CPCB equivalent is cited. (3) The NITI/TERI 6.19 Mt (2024) and 14 MMT (2030) figures, and the supporting stats (10% formal vs 22% global, 62% informal, 2,808 collection centres, 1.75 Mt capacity, 400+ recyclers, Rs 51,000 crore, 18% value captured) are all not confirmed by snippet; the '22% global' figure matches GEM 2024's 22.3% formal collection/recycling rate for 2022, and GEM 2024's India 4.1 Mt (2022) figure is consistent with my knowledge. (4) EY-Parthenon 'USD 32 bn waste-management market (2023)', MRAI '65 Mt scrap demand by 2030, half domestic', and MRAI 'non-ferrous USD 18 bn to 30 bn' are analyst/trade-body figures cited to secondary press (The Core, ANI, Metals-Hub) and none was confirmed by snippet; the 65 Mt figure is also easily confused with the Ministry of Steel's own steel-scrap demand projections, so it needs the original MRAI wording. (5) Waste-picker range 1.5-4 million and the NAMASTE 2.5 lakh enumeration target are consistent with my knowledge (ILO/AIW 1.5 m; Cabinet added waste pickers to NAMASTE in June 2024 with a 2.5 lakh profiling target) but not confirmed by snippet. (6) Arithmetic checks: 13,97,955.59 t = 1.398 Mt (ok); 9.79/14.14 = 69.2% (ok); 1.4/6.19 = 22.6%, so 'roughly a quarter' is fair (ok). (7) Refined-chain gap: the deck's TAM framing covers only municipal scrap and e-waste. The founder's 30 Sep 2026 model adds pre-processors, compounders, five price levels (L1-L5) and 400+ industrial by-products (bagasse, fly ash, slag, dross, foundry sand, husk, whey) as candidate listings, which is a separate and much larger tonnage pool (fly ash alone is in the hundreds of Mt a year per CEA reports) that the answer's 'bottom-up Bengaluru tonnage-times-price' model must either include or explicitly exclude.
verdicts.correction: Keep the core framing (both numbers measure different things; lead with the regulator's figure, show NITI's as a modelled upper bound) but change three things. First, the CPCB slide must state which official series it uses, because two exist: the older MoEFCC series (10.14 lakh t in 2019-20 to 17.51 lakh t in 2023-24, Rajya Sabha reply, Dec 2024) and the newer EPR-portal series cited in the 11 Aug 2025 Lok Sabha reply (12.54 lakh t FY2023-24, 13.98 lakh t FY2024-25, and reportedly 14.14 lakh t generated / 9.79 lakh t recycled, about 69%, for FY2025-26 per a March 2026 PTI report). Use the newer series and footnote the older one, otherwise an investor's own search contradicts the deck. Second, label every NITI/TERI statistic (6.19 Mt 2024, 14 MMT 2030, 10% formal vs 22% global, 62% informal, 2,808 centres, 1.75 Mt capacity, Rs 51,000 crore, 18% captured) as 'NITI Aayog/TERI, Jan 2026, modelled' and re-confirm each against the PDF before the deck goes out; the only figures I can vouch for from knowledge are GEM 2024's India 4.1 Mt (2022) and its 22.3% global formal rate. Third, for market size say plainly that there is no official India recycling-market number; quote analyst figures (EY-Parthenon USD 32 bn waste management 2023; MRAI 65 Mt scrap demand by 2030; MRAI non-ferrous USD 18 bn to 30 bn) only with source and year, and re-confirm each against the original MRAI/EY wording, since none was confirmed in this pass. Build the deck's own TAM bottom-up along the refined chain: Bengaluru household tonnage at L1 prices, plus the L2-L5 trade layers (yard, pre-processor, recycler/compounder, manufacturer), plus a separately stated industrial by-product pool (fly ash, slag, bagasse etc. mapped to KSPCB category codes) that is either included with its own tonnage source or explicitly parked. For waste pickers keep '1.5-4 million, no official count (ILO/AIW 1.5 m; Chintan up to 4 m), with NAMASTE targeting 2.5 lakh enumerated'. Status should stay 'partly'; open items: confirm the FY2025-26 pair from a PIB or CPCB page rather than a wire story; obtain the Dec 2024 PIB release to footnote the 17.51 lakh t series; confirm every NITI/TERI and MRAI/EY figure by snippet or by opening the PDFs when network access is restored.

verdicts.question: Recommend defaults with reasoning for the founders' open product decisions: pickup charges or minimum load; recycle points value and CSR funding; zero-value items earning points; excluding batteries and e-waste from the household pilot; auto-accept limited to shop hours; a no-show rule; Saathi accident insurance options and cost; business fees after the pilot.
verdicts.problems: VERIFICATION STATUS: none of the 25 cited sources could be confirmed by snippet in this pass (search budget exhausted, fetches refused); this is a knowledge-based audit. Claims consistent with my knowledge (but not confirmed by snippet): MCA General Circular 14/2021 of 25 Aug 2021 and its exclusions (normal course of business, employee benefit, marketing sponsorship, statutory obligations) and implementing-agency rules (Section 8 company/trust/society with 12A and 80G, three-year record, CSR-1); E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 notified 2 Nov 2022, in force 1 Apr 2023, 106 items, Rule 8 bulk-consumer and Rule 9 recycler duties; PMSBY Rs 20 a year for Rs 2 lakh (Rs 1 lakh partial), ages 18-70, w.e.f. 1 Jun 2022; Code on Social Security 2020 in force 21 Nov 2025 with 1-2% aggregator contribution capped at 5% of payouts; EPR certificate price band 30-100% of environmental compensation (E-Waste Second Amendment Rules 2024). Problems found: (1) Internal inconsistency: the answer says the Karnataka welfare fee applies 'since 16 Feb 2026' while its own source title says 'effective 13 Feb 2026'; the per-transaction caps (Rs 0.50/0.75/1.00) and the 30 May 2025 commencement are not confirmed by snippet. (2) Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 are dated 22 Aug 2022 (G.S.R. 650(E)); 24 Aug 2022 is the PIB announcement date, not the notification date. (3) Points design has a regulatory hole: RBI's PPI Master Directions (2021) leave closed-system PPIs unregulated only when they are redeemable for the issuer's own goods and services; points redeemable for third-party 'partner vouchers' look semi-closed, which needs RBI authorisation or a loyalty-programme structure where Luma.Green buys and gifts the vouchers. The answer routes this to counsel but recommends partner vouchers as a default. (4) The CSR point slightly overstates: a company may also route CSR through a Section 8 company it or another company established (the three-year track record then does not apply), so a Luma.Green-linked Section 8 vehicle is a possible route the answer omits. (5) Newer development not checked: CPCB's EPR floor prices for e-waste certificates (2025) were challenged by producers in the Delhi High Court; the outcome affects the 'EPR-obligated producers are the natural per-kg funders' line and was not searched. (6) All price-card figures (The Kabadiwala Bangalore rates, ScrapBuddy Rs 200 floor and Rs 3/kg glass, KabadiwalaOnline Rs 999/Rs 499, Rs 5/kg multilayer), all insurance figures (Ditto Rs 0.45 per Rs 1,000, Plum Rs 100-600, Bharatsure Rs 69/month) and all fee comparables (IndiaMART Rs 28k/45k/60k, Udaan 0.5-2%, JioMart 1-15%, Amazon Business from 2%) are unconfirmed and several are dated 29 Sep 2026 as live pages that were not opened; the IndiaMART figures come from a Feb 2024 third-party blog and are likely stale. (7) Arithmetic checks pass: Rs 150-200 at Rs 10/kg = 15-20 kg; Rs 0.45 per Rs 1,000 on Rs 10 lakh = Rs 450. (8) Refined-chain gaps: the e-waste phase-2 plan should name the dismantler as a pre-processor (S4 stripped) with a CPCB/KSPCB registration number on every trade and a processing record whose residuals (PCB fractions, hazardous dust) go to a TSDF; the fee model should say which of the five price levels it applies to (L2-L5 buyer side, with pre-processors and compounders as new fee-paying buyers) and whether the industrial by-product marketplace (bagasse, fly ash, slag, GST-invoiced buyers) carries a different fee or tier; zero-value items should be recorded as S1/S2 lots with an L1 price of zero so the points ledger stays separate from the price ledger.
verdicts.correction: Keep the defaults but fix the following. Points: 1 point = Re 1, about 5% of scrap value, capped, never cash, funded by Luma.Green, and redeemable only for Luma.Green's own benefits (pickup bonus, priority slots, branded goods) until counsel confirms that redemption at third-party partners does not make the programme a semi-closed PPI under RBI's Master Directions on Prepaid Payment Instruments (2021); if partner rewards are wanted, structure them as Luma.Green-purchased gift vouchers issued under the loyalty programme, not as points spendable at partners. CSR: still not a funder of points; add the option of a Section 8 company (established by Luma.Green or a partner company, no three-year track record needed in that case) as the vehicle for Saathi welfare spend, alongside a registered NGO with 12A/80G and CSR-1. Batteries and e-waste: exclude from the household pilot; in phase 2 route household e-waste to a KSPCB/CPCB-registered dismantler modelled as a pre-processor (state S4 stripped), record its registration number on every trade, and store each dismantling record with main output, saleable by-products and residual waste sent to a TSDF; cite the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 as notified 22 Aug 2022 (G.S.R. 650(E)); before relying on EPR-certificate money as a collection funder, check the status of the producers' Delhi High Court challenge to CPCB's 2025 e-waste EPR floor prices. Insurance: PMSBY (Rs 20 a year, Rs 2 lakh) at onboarding plus a group PA policy; treat the Rs 300-600 plus GST per head budget as a placeholder until a broker quote, since no premium figure was confirmed. Gig law: Code on Social Security 2020 in force 21 Nov 2025 (contribution start date to be confirmed) and Karnataka's Platform Based Gig Workers Act 2025 with a 1% welfare fee; resolve the 13 vs 16 Feb 2026 effective-date inconsistency from the gazette notification itself and confirm with counsel whether a scrap-collection platform falls within the Act's listed aggregator sectors. Fees: kabadiwalas free; yards, pre-processors, recyclers, compounders and manufacturers free in the pilot, then 0.5-1% per trade charged to the buyer side at price levels L2-L5, capped per trade, with an optional paid tier for verification, traceability and EPR documentation; decide separately whether industrial by-product listings (bagasse, fly ash, slag etc.) carry a listing fee or a higher tier, since those buyers are GST-invoiced industrial firms. Re-confirm every price-card, insurance and marketplace-fee figure by snippet before it is shown to anyone; status stays 'needs-pilot-or-counsel'.
